## Network git and gh commands

The sandbox blocks GitHub. Run all commands that need the network (git pull, git fetch, git push, git clone, gh issue, gh pr, gh api) through the Terminal panel (run_in_terminal), not the sandbox shell. Don't try the sandbox first or ask me before doing this. Local-only git commands (status, log, diff, branch, commit) can stay in the sandbox.

## Before starting

- Read the repo's AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md and follow it. Repo-level rules override this file.
- Run `git status` and `git fetch` (via the terminal) first. If the working tree has unrelated uncommitted changes, stop and tell me instead of mixing them in.
- If the task maps to an issue, read it with `gh issue view` and reference it in the branch, commits and PR.

## Branches

- Never commit directly to `main`, `master` or `dev`. Always work on a new branch.
- Branch from the latest `dev` (fall back to the repo's default branch if there is no `dev`) unless I say otherwise.
- Name: `<type>/<issue-number>-<short-kebab-description>`, e.g. `fix/123-login-redirect-loop`. Drop the issue number if there isn't one.
- Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`.

## Commits

- Always use Conventional Commits: `<type>(<optional scope>): <description>`
- Imperative mood, lowercase, no trailing period, subject line under 72 characters.
- Use the same types as branches. Mark breaking changes with `!` after the type/scope and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.
- Add a body only when the "why" isn't obvious from the diff. Reference issues in the footer (`Refs #123`; `Closes #123` only in the PR).
- Keep commits small and atomic: one logical change each, with the repo passing at every commit.
- Never use `--no-verify`, never amend or rewrite commits that have been pushed, and never add co-author or "generated by" trailers unless I ask.
- Never force push. If a push is rejected, fetch and rebase, and tell me if there are conflicts.

## Pull requests

- Open PRs with `gh pr create --base dev --body-file <file>`. Use a body file, not inline `--body`, so formatting survives.
- If the repo has `.github/pull_request_template.md` (or similar), use it and fill in every section. Otherwise use this:

```
  ## Summary
  What changed and why, in 1-3 sentences.

  ## Changes
  - Key change 1
  - Key change 2

  ## How to test
  Steps or commands to verify.

  ## Screenshots
  Before / after (UI changes only, otherwise remove this section).

  ## Diagram
  Mermaid diagram (non-trivial changes only, otherwise remove this section).

  ## Notes
  Risks, follow-ups, migrations, config changes.

  Closes #<issue>
```

- PR title follows Conventional Commits, same as the commits.
- PRs that change UI include before/after screenshots. If you can't upload images from the CLI, save them to a known path, leave a clear placeholder in the PR and tell me where the files are.
- Non-trivial PRs include a Mermaid diagram (flow, sequence or architecture, whichever fits).
- Keep PRs focused. If you spot unrelated problems, note them for me or open a separate issue instead of widening the PR.
- Before opening a PR: lint, type-check and the full relevant test suite pass, and you've reviewed your own diff with `git diff <base>...HEAD`.

## Code quality

- Prefer quality, simplicity and long term maintainability over development speed.
- Match the existing code style, structure and naming of the repo. Don't introduce new dependencies or patterns without a reason, and explain the reason in the PR.
- Don't leave debug code, commented-out code, stray TODOs or unrelated formatting changes in the diff.
- Never commit secrets, tokens, `.env` files or generated artifacts. If you find one already committed, tell me.

## Testing and bug fixes

- Bug fixes: reproduce the bug end to end first, then add a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after.
- New behavior comes with tests. Don't delete or weaken existing tests to make them pass.
- Fix lint errors, failing tests and flaky tests you come across, in separate commits (`chore`, `test` or `fix`), not mixed into feature commits.

## Wrapping up

- Clean up dev servers and background processes before you finish.
- Keep reports short: what changed, what was verified, anything I need to decide or follow up on. Include the PR link if one was opened.
- If something is blocked or ambiguous, say so briefly instead of guessing at a risky action (destructive git operations, deleting data, changing CI or config).

## Topic notes (shared memory)

Since 2026-11-18 the main copy of the topic notes is on the Mini, kept by the
Claude coordinator there: `~/.claude/projects/<coord-dir-slug>/memory/`
(read with `~/.local/bin/hc exec --on mac-mini -- cat <path>`). The memory
folder on this MacBook is an old snapshot. Rules for the notes:

- When we work on an ongoing topic (a bug hunt, a deploy problem, a feature
  across sessions), keep one note for it: `topic-<slug>.md` in the memory
  folder, `type: project`, with the current state, decisions and why, what was
  tried and failed, open questions and next steps. Use absolute dates.
- Update it as things change, not only at the end: a session can stop at any
  time. Rewrite it to the current state instead of appending a log.
- Keep one line per topic in `MEMORY.md`. When I mention a topic, read its note
  before answering.
- When a topic is finished, say so in the note, or delete it once nothing in it
  is still useful.

## Coordinating with Claude and Codex

When you coordinate project work (delegating to the Mac mini, or working
alongside the other coordinator), follow `~/projects/CLAUDE.md`,
section "Claude and Codex", the one canonical policy for both coordinators.
If you were started outside `~/projects`, read that file first.
